title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 427
paragraphs: When Apis had ended his life from the wound, the priests buried him without Cambyses's knowledge. But Cambyses, as the Egyptians say, immediately after this evil deed became completely mad — not having been really in his right senses even before that time. The first of his evil deeds was to put to death his brother Smerdis, who was his brother by the same father and same mother. This brother he had sent away from Egypt to Persia out of envy, because Smerdis alone of all the Persians had been able to draw the bow which the Ichthyophagoi brought from the Ethiopian king, to the extent of about two finger-breadths, while none of the other Persians had proved able to do so. Then when Smerdis had gone off to Persia, Cambyses saw a vision in his sleep of this kind: it seemed to him that a messenger came from Persia and reported that Smerdis, sitting upon the royal throne, had touched the heavens with his head. Fearing therefore lest his brother should kill him and reign in his place, he sent Prexaspes to Persia — the man he trusted most of all the Persians — with orders to kill him. Prexaspes accordingly went up to Susa and killed Smerdis; some say he took him out on a hunt and killed him there, others that he brought him to the Erythraian Sea and drowned him.
